clinicalPearls: Excessive numbers of bacteria in the small intestine causing bloating, flatulence, diarrhoea and, when severe, malabsorption
It is a consequence of impaired clearance of small-bowel bacteria rather than a communicable infection
Predisposing factors include disordered motility, anatomical changes such as blind loops and strictures, and loss of protective gastric acid
Severe or long-standing cases can cause fat and vitamin B12 malabsorption with weight loss and deficiency
Breath testing after a carbohydrate load is commonly used, though it has recognised limitations
Treatment combines antibiotics with correction of the underlying predisposing factor where possible
reference.pathophysiology: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth develops when the mechanisms that normally keep the small-bowel bacterial population low, principally propulsive motility, gastric acid and an intact ileocaecal valve, are impaired. Overgrowth of predominantly colonic-type bacteria in the small bowel leads to fermentation of carbohydrates, producing gas and bloating, deconjugation of bile salts causing fat malabsorption, and competition for and altered handling of nutrients such as vitamin B12. It is therefore a disorder of dysbiosis and impaired clearance secondary to motility or structural abnormalities, not a primary infective disease.
additionalInvestigations: Carbohydrate breath testing (for example glucose or lactulose)
Assessment for underlying motility disorders or anatomical abnormalities
Nutritional studies including vitamin B12 and fat-soluble vitamins in suspected malabsorption
Coeliac serology and pancreatic assessment to exclude mimics
Small-bowel imaging where structural causes are suspected
redFlags: Weight loss and features of malabsorption
An underlying structural lesion such as a stricture or fistula
Failure to respond to appropriate treatment
reference.prognosis: Symptoms usually improve with antibiotic treatment, but recurrence is common when the underlying predisposing factor persists, so addressing the cause is important for durable control.
pitfalls: Diagnosing it on symptoms alone given overlap with irritable bowel syndrome
Treating recurrent episodes without addressing the underlying motility or anatomical cause
Over-reliance on breath tests despite their limitations
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Antibiotic therapy, commonly rifaximin or alternatives such as tetracyclines, metronidazole or co-amoxiclav, to reduce the small-bowel bacterial load.
Correct the underlying predisposing factor where possible, whether a motility disorder, an anatomical blind loop or stricture, or loss of protective gastric acid.
Replace nutritional deficiencies, notably vitamin B12 and fat-soluble vitamins, and optimise nutrition in malabsorption.
Consider prokinetic agents to improve small-bowel clearance and reduce recurrence in dysmotility.
Surgical correction of amenable anatomical abnormalities such as strictures or blind loops.
Monitor for symptom recurrence and repeat or cycle antibiotics where the predisposing cause persists.
Refer to gastroenterology for refractory or recurrent disease and to investigate an underlying cause.
